newsitem.title: SPAIN: Azucarera sale paves way for Spain sugar shake-up.
newsitem.headline: Azucarera sale paves way for Spain sugar shake-up.

text.p: Spain's leading sugar producer Ebro Agricola's purchase of a stake in fellow producer Azucarera marks the first step toward a merger and sets up a shake-up in the sector, analysts said on Tuesday.

Banco Central Hispano sold a 21.8 percent stake in Azucarera to Ebro as part of a plan to dispose of its 49.9 percent shareholding, according to a statement issued by the Stock Market Commission CNMV on Monday.
The bank also sold 24 percent of the sugar group to Caja de Salamanca, a savings group with sugar interests that has made public its desire to secure Azucarera as a customer.
"Ebro's purchase represents the first move toward a merger of the two groups," said Agustin Mazuecos, analyst at ABN-Amro in Madrid. "Ebro bought the shares at a good price too."
ABN-Amro said it had valued Ebro's 21.8 percent stake in Azucarera at a considerably higher level than that implied by the price Ebro paid.

BCH sold its shares for 5,213 pesetas per share, valuing the sale to Ebro at 9.35 billion pesetas, and valuing Azucarera as a whole at 43.76 billion pesetas. Mazuecos said his value of Azucarera was 46.35 billion pesetas.

Full integration of the two companies would produce a virtual monopoly on Spain's sugar production with over 80 percent of the country's EU quota and would become the fifth largest sugar producer in the EU.
Analysts said a merger would reap considerable cost savings and bring a long needed shake-up to the sugar sector.

"A merger would accelerate the restructuring process that the Spanish sector needs so badly to be competitive in Europe," said an analyst at a bank in Madrid. "We will still be less competitive than other countries in Europe but we will have a strong group that will be much more defensive".
The Spanish sugar sector has suffered from duplication of sugar production plants which has stifled productivity.

"The unified production system would allow at least five more plants to be closed which in turn would considerably boost the cost-cutting potential of each company," ABN-Amro said in a reserach document, adding that it had valued the cost savings for Azucarera at 7.38 billion pesetas.

Analysts said Ebro's purchase also implied that the sugar sector would remain in Spanish hands much to the delight of the Ministry of Agriculture which has previously blocked attempts by foreign firms to control production.
The ministry frustrated attempts by France's Saint-Louis to increase its 20.35 percent stake in Azucarera, but analysts said the company would want to maintain this level in the merged company.
"In the event of a merger, Saint Louis's stake will be reduced and it will probably want to increase its share back up to over 20 percent," said one analyst.
But analysts pointed out that attempts to increase its stake in the new company significantly above 20 percent would meet the continued opposition of the Ministry of Agriculture.

Analysts were unsure of the exact make-up of other shareholders in the event of a merger. The Kuwait Investment Office is Ebro's largest shareholder with a 35 percent stake, followed by Spain's leading domestic banking group Banco Santander with a 14.38 percent share.

Analysts said they expected state-owned food group Mercasa, who initially made an offer for a share of BCH's stake, to buy the banks' remaining 4.1 percent at a later date. Mercasa already holds a 4.7 percent share in Ebro.

Azucarera's shares have risen 13 percent since late August in anticipation of the sale of BCH's holding and most analysts said they expected shares to remain steady for the time being. At 1500 GMT on Tuesday shares stood at 5,140, up 10 pesetas.
But Ebro' shares were marginally weaker on Tuesday, down 20 pesetas at 1,695, although most analysts said there was certainly room for improvement.
